title: Gentle with the ledger
hookLine: Seneca reviews his day without hiding anything, then tells himself: see that you don't do it again, this time I forgive you (On Anger 3.36)

cards: Around one in the morning, the replay starts, uninvited. The awkward thing you said at lunch. The email you sent too fast.
The thing you should have said to your mother in 2014. For some people, that's what evening review means, and their stomach drops at the words. But it isn't a review.
It's a trial with no defense lawyer and no end. If that's you, this story is for you, because Seneca describes his own review, and it has something the 1am trial never has. A pardon.

teach.b: In the same passage from On Anger, right after Sextius's questions, Seneca tells what he does himself.
Each night, when the light is out, he goes over the whole day, and he says he hides nothing from himself and passes over nothing.

Why should he fear any of his mistakes, he asks, when he can say to himself, in paraphrase: see that you don't do that again; this time, I forgive you. Then come his examples, and they're wonderfully ordinary.

You argued too hotly in that discussion; next time, don't pick a fight with people who don't know better. You warned that man more frankly than you should have, and you didn't help him, you offended him.
Next time, think about whether what you say is true, and also whether the person can bear to hear it. Look at the shape. Seneca is honest: he doesn't pretend the argument went fine.
He draws a lesson for next time.
And he closes the ledger with a pardon. Not a shrug, not an excuse: a forgiveness that comes after the honesty, not instead of it. That's what the 1am trial is missing.
It keeps reopening the case because nobody ever rules. Seneca rules. Guilty, lesson noted, forgiven, go to sleep.
A review without the forgiveness turns into punishment, and punishment can make people hide from their faults rather than mend them. A review with it makes the next night's honesty easier.
It's what lets you keep looking.

how: People who keep a Stoic evening review often follow Seneca's pattern from On Anger 3.36: go over the day honestly, name what went wrong, note what to do next time, and end by letting it go.

games.q: what's inside Seneca's ledger — tap the pairs.
p: don't fight with those who don't know better

s: Seneca's review skipped over his faults to stay positive
he says he hides nothing from himself and passes over nothing.
Seneca ends his review by forgiving himself
see that you don't do that again; this time, I forgive you.
forgiving yourself means pretending it went fine
Seneca names the fault exactly first. the pardon comes after the honesty, not instead of it.

games.q: you're Seneca. you've gone over the day and found you argued too hotly and hurt a man with frank advice. how do you end the review?
o: replay it until you fall asleep.
decide it wasn't really your fault.
draw a lesson, then forgive yourself this time.
games.why: he names it, draws a lesson for next time, and closes with: this time, I forgive you.

practice: Pick one moment from the last day you're not proud of, a sharp word, a thing left undone, and name it plainly, the way Seneca does: you did this.
Find the lesson, next time, I'll try this instead, then close it the way he does: this time, you're forgiven. Say it inside, notice what your shoulders do, and let the case be closed.

wordCard.voice: Ignosco. Latin for I forgive: Seneca's word at the end of an honest review of the day, so it can end at all. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: I forgive, I pardon. Seneca's word at the end of his nightly review.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiven this time. If the 1am trial starts up later, the case is already closed. Day one hundred six, done.
